newsitem.title: USA: Jewell considering suit against CNN - attorney.
newsitem.headline: Jewell considering suit against CNN - attorney.

text.p: Former Olympic bomb suspect Richard Jewell is considering whether to sue Cable News Network over its coverage of the investigation into last summer's bombing at the Atlanta Olympics, a Jewell attorney said on Friday.

Lin Wood, one of two attorneys retained by Jewell to handle libel suits against the news media, said he has met with CNN executives to discuss coverage of the security guard's role as the only named suspect in the investigation.

The Wall Street Journal reported in an article on Friday that Jewell's attorneys had spoken to CNN about a possible out-of-court settlement. The talks followed a deal with NBC valued at more than $500,000, according to the newspaper.
In New York, NBC declined to comment on the reported settlement figure. "We're not confirming that number," NBC spokeswoman Beth Comstock said.
Wood said Jewell has not yet decided whether CNN's coverage would merit legal action. Wood also declined to comment on the reported settlement with NBC.

"We are looking at CNN's coverage because we know their coverage was extensive. So, we haven't ruled them in or out at this point in time. We're still looking at the coverage," Wood told Reuters in an interview.
"We've talked to a number of people, including CNN, just in general about their coverage of the Richard Jewell story and some concerns that we have about it."
A spokesman for CNN, which is a unit of the giant media company Time Warner Inc., declined to comment.

Jewell's attorneys have vowed to investigate every news organization that covered his role in an FBI investigation that included a massive search of his Atlanta home. He also is considering lawsuits against the federal government and individual agents.
So far, his attorneys have brought a lawsuit against an Atlanta radio station for using Jewell's image in billboard advertisements without his permission.
Wood said he planned to bring suit against the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and a Georgia college where Jewell once worked as a campus police officer by the end of this month.

The July pipe-bomb explosion came at a crowded outdoor concert in downtown Atlanta, and left two people dead and more than 100 wounded. Jewell, now 34, was on duty as a security guard at a nearby corporate pavillion at the time.
Initially, he was hailed as a hero for spotting the knapsack that contained the bomb and helping to clear people from the area before it detonated.
But three days later, the Atlanta Journal published an article naming him as a suspect in the investigation.
Jewell spent the next three months being hounded by the news media and the FBI. Then, in October, the Justice Department publicly cleared him of suspicion.
